Let $x^*$ be a strict local minimum of $V_0$ and let the tolerances $\varepsilon_r$, $\varepsilon_v$ be given, with $\varepsilon_r$ small enough that $V_0(x)$ is larger than $V_0(x^*)$ for every $x \neq x^*$ with $\lvert x - x^*\rvert \leq \varepsilon_r$. Define the depth of the well at that distance and a target margin:

$$\begin{aligned} \Delta V &= \min\left\{V_0(x^* - \varepsilon_r),\ V_0(x^* + \varepsilon_r)\right\} - V_0(x^*) > 0 \quad &\text{(strict minimum)} \\ E_0 - V_0(x^*) &= \tfrac12\,m\,\dot x(0)^2 + V_0\big(x(0)\big) - V_0(x^*) \quad &\text{(energy of the initial state, Eq. 4.26)} \\ &< \tfrac12\,m\,\delta_v^2 + \left[V_0\big(x(0)\big) - V_0(x^*)\right] \quad &\text{(initial speed below $\delta_v$)} \\ &< \min\left\{\Delta V,\ \tfrac12\,m\,\varepsilon_v^2\right\} \quad &\text{(choose $\delta_v$ and $\delta_r \leq \varepsilon_r$ small enough; $V_0$ is continuous at $x^*$)} \\ V_0\big(x(t)\big) &\leq E_0 < V_0(x^*) + \Delta V \quad &\text{(allowed region, Eq. 4.28, at every $t > 0$; previous row)} \\ \lvert x(t) - x^*\rvert &< \varepsilon_r \quad &\text{($x(t)$ is continuous, starts inside and cannot reach $x^* \pm \varepsilon_r$, where $V_0 \geq V_0(x^*) + \Delta V$)} \\ \tfrac12\,m\,\dot x(t)^2 &= E_0 - V_0\big(x(t)\big) \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.27)} \\ &\leq E_0 - V_0(x^*) \quad &\text{(inside the interval $V_0 \geq V_0(x^*)$)} \\ &< \tfrac12\,m\,\varepsilon_v^2 \quad &\text{(choice of the initial perturbation)} \\ \lvert\dot x(t)\rvert &< \varepsilon_v \quad &\text{(divide by $m/2$ and take the square root)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\lvert x(0) - x^*\rvert < \delta_r,\ \lvert\dot x(0)\rvert < \delta_v \ \Longrightarrow\ \lvert x(t) - x^*\rvert < \varepsilon_r,\ \lvert\dot x(t)\rvert < \varepsilon_v \ \ \forall\,t > 0}$$

Units: energies in $\mathrm J$, distances in $\mathrm m$, speeds in $\mathrm{m/s}$; $\tfrac12\,m\,\varepsilon_v^2$ is in $\mathrm{kg\,(m/s)^2} = \mathrm J$

Meaning: a particle started close to the bottom of a well with a small speed has too little energy to climb out of it, and its speed stays small because the gap between $E_0$ and the curve stays small: this is the definition of stability of [Lecture 2, Slide 21], and it shows the notes' criterion, stable at a minimum of the potential, from the energy alone (Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.6).

Small motions about an equilibrium: oscillation or departure Law: equation of motion with the force expanded to first order; characteristic equation of a linear equation with constant coefficients Source: Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.6; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.21; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.7; [Lecture 2, Slide 22]

The stiffness at the equilibrium is the second derivative of the potential there; $C_1$, $C_2$ are integration constants and $\xi_0$, $\dot\xi_0$ the initial displacement and velocity.

$$\begin{aligned} m\,\ddot\xi &= -\frac{d^2V_0}{dx^2}(x^*)\,\xi \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.21 with the first-order force of the box above; $\ddot x = \ddot\xi$ because $x^*$ is constant)} \\ \xi &= \exp(p\,t) \quad &\text{(trial solution of a linear equation with constant coefficients)} \\ \dot\xi &= p\exp(p\,t) \quad &\text{(chain rule: the derivative of the exponent is $p$)} \\ \ddot\xi &= p^2\exp(p\,t) \quad &\text{(chain rule again)} \\ m\,p^2\exp(p\,t) &= -\frac{d^2V_0}{dx^2}(x^*)\exp(p\,t) \quad &\text{(substitute the trial solution and its second derivative)} \\ m\,p^2 + \frac{d^2V_0}{dx^2}(x^*) &= 0 \quad &\text{(divide by the exponential, never zero: characteristic equation)} \\ p &= \pm\,i\sqrt{\frac{d^2V_0/dx^2(x^*)}{m}} \quad &\text{(minimum: positive second derivative, two imaginary roots)} \\ \omega_0 &= \sqrt{\frac{d^2V_0/dx^2(x^*)}{m}} \quad &\text{(name the modulus of the two roots)} \\ m\,\omega_0^2 &= \frac{d^2V_0}{dx^2}(x^*) \quad &\text{(square and multiply by $m$)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\cos(\omega_0 t) &= -\omega_0\sin(\omega_0 t) \quad &\text{(chain rule: the derivative of $\omega_0 t$ is $\omega_0$)} \\ \frac{d^2}{dt^2}\cos(\omega_0 t) &= -\omega_0^2\cos(\omega_0 t) \quad &\text{(chain rule again)} \\ m\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\cos(\omega_0 t) + \frac{d^2V_0}{dx^2}(x^*)\cos(\omega_0 t) &= \left(-m\,\omega_0^2 + \frac{d^2V_0}{dx^2}(x^*)\right)\cos(\omega_0 t) \quad &\text{(substitute $\xi = \cos(\omega_0 t)$ in the first row, written with every term on the left)} \\ &= 0 \quad &\text{(the row with $m\,\omega_0^2$: the cosine is a real solution)} \\ \frac{d^2}{dt^2}\sin(\omega_0 t) &= -\omega_0^2\sin(\omega_0 t) \quad &\text{(chain rule twice: the same steps, so the sine is a solution too)} \\ \xi &= C_1\cos(\omega_0 t) + C_2\sin(\omega_0 t) \quad &\text{(the equation is linear and homogeneous: any combination of two solutions is one; two constants for a second-order equation, as in Section 8, Eq. 5.7)} \\ p &= \pm\,p_1,\quad p_1 = \sqrt{\frac{-d^2V_0/dx^2(x^*)}{m}} > 0 \quad &\text{(maximum: negative second derivative, two real roots)} \\ \xi &= C_1\exp(p_1 t) + C_2\exp(-p_1 t) \quad &\text{(general solution with two real roots)} \\ \dot\xi &= p_1 C_1\exp(p_1 t) - p_1 C_2\exp(-p_1 t) \quad &\text{(differentiate; chain rule on each exponential)} \\ \xi_0 &= C_1 + C_2,\qquad \dot\xi_0 = p_1\left(C_1 - C_2\right) \quad &\text{(both rows at $t = 0$)} \\ C_1 &= \tfrac12\left(\xi_0 + \frac{\dot\xi_0}{p_1}\right) \quad &\text{(add the first equation to the second divided by $p_1$, then halve)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\text{minimum: } \xi = C_1\cos(\omega_0 t) + C_2\sin(\omega_0 t);\qquad \text{maximum: } \xi = C_1\exp(p_1 t) + C_2\exp(-p_1 t),\ \ C_1 = \tfrac12\left(\xi_0 + \dot\xi_0/p_1\right)}$$

Units: $\omega_0$ and $p_1$ in $\sqrt{(\mathrm{N/m})/\mathrm{kg}} = \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, so their products with $t$ are dimensionless; $C_1$, $C_2$ in $\mathrm m$

Meaning: at a minimum the linearised motion is a bounded oscillation about the equilibrium, a harmonic oscillator (Chapter 5). At a maximum every perturbation with $C_1 \neq 0$, which is every perturbation except those with the initial velocity exactly $-p_1\xi_0$, grows like $\exp(p_1 t)$ and carries the particle away, so the equilibrium is unstable; the linear model holds only while $\xi$ is small, which is enough to show the departure. A full treatment of linearisation about an equilibrium is given with the harmonic oscillator (Lecture 6).

When the second derivative is zero

If the second derivative of $V_0$ vanishes at the equilibrium, the first-order force is zero and the boxes above decide nothing: the sign of the force near $x^*$, and with it the stability, is then set by the higher-order terms of the expansion of $V_0$. In two and three dimensions the equilibria are the points where the gradient of $V_0$ vanishes, and an equilibrium is stable if and only if it is a local minimum of the potential energy, which is checked with the second derivatives of $V_0$ (Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.6).

Figure 11. Equilibria are the critical points of $V_0$; at a minimum the force crosses zero with negative slope and restores, at a maximum with positive slope and repels ([Lecture 2, Slide 22])..

7. The simple pendulum

The simple pendulum illustrates the conservation of mechanical energy and the kind of analysis it allows (Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.7; [Lecture 2, Slide 23]): kinematics and dynamics of this simple system, the discussion of its energy, and the linearisation of its equation of motion.

The simple pendulum (Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.7, Fig. 4.3; [Lecture 2, Slide 23])

Example

A bob of mass $m$ hangs from a fixed point $O$ of the inertial frame $S_0$ by a light rigid rod of length $\ell$ and negligible mass, and moves in the vertical plane $Oxy$ under gravity, with $Oy$ vertical and upwards. The problem is solved in polar coordinates $(R, \theta)$, with the angle $\theta$ measured from the downward vertical, the direction of $-Oy$, positive counterclockwise, and with the local basis $\{\mathbf e_R, \mathbf e_\theta\}$ of Notes.pdf, Sec. 2.6.2. Since the distance from $O$ is the constant $\ell$, the problem has a single degree of freedom, the coordinate $\theta$.

DataValue
frame$S_0$, inertial; $\mathbf i$ horizontal to the right, $\mathbf j$ vertical upwards, $\mathbf k$ out of the paper
bobmass $m$, at distance $R = \ell$ from $O$ (constant)
gravity$\mathbf g = -g\,\mathbf j$
coordinate$\theta$, from $-\mathbf j$ to the rod, counterclockwise
Figure 12. Simple pendulum of length $\ell$ and mass $m$: the angle $\theta$ is measured from the downward vertical, so $x = \ell\sin\theta$, $y = -\ell\cos\theta$ and $\theta_{\mathrm{pol}} = \theta - \pi/2$ (Notes.pdf Fig. 4.3; [Lecture 2, Slide 23])..

Position, basis and kinematics

The angle from the vertical and the standard polar angle Law: right triangle of the rod with the vertical; cylindrical coordinates; angle subtraction formulas Source: Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.7; Notes.pdf Fig. 4.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.23

Main plane, $\mathbf k$ out of the paper (⊙): the bob $P$, the pivot $O$ and the foot $H$ of the perpendicular from $P$ to the vertical through $O$ form a right triangle, right-angled at $H$, with hypotenuse $OP$ of length $\ell$ and the angle $\theta$ at $O$, between the downward vertical $OH$ and the rod. $\theta_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the standard polar angle of $P$, measured from $Ox$ counterclockwise, as in Eq. 2.23.

$$\begin{aligned} x &= \ell\sin\theta \quad &\text{(leg $HP$, opposite to $\theta$, horizontal and to the right for $\theta > 0$)} \\ y &= -\ell\cos\theta \quad &\text{(leg $OH$, adjacent to $\theta$, pointing along $-\mathbf j$)} \\ x &= \ell\cos\theta_{\mathrm{pol}},\quad y = \ell\sin\theta_{\mathrm{pol}} \quad &\text{(standard polar coordinates of $P$, Eq. 2.23 with $R = \ell$)} \\ \cos\left(\theta - \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) &= \cos\theta\cos\tfrac{\pi}{2} + \sin\theta\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2} \quad &\text{(cosine of a difference)} \\ &= \sin\theta \quad &\text{($\cos\tfrac{\pi}{2} = 0$, $\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2} = 1$)} \\ \sin\left(\theta - \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) &= \sin\theta\cos\tfrac{\pi}{2} - \cos\theta\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2} \quad &\text{(sine of a difference)} \\ &= -\cos\theta \quad &\text{(the same values)} \\ \theta_{\mathrm{pol}} &= \theta - \tfrac{\pi}{2} \quad &\text{(this angle gives the same $x$ and $y$ as the triangle, both rows)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{x = \ell\sin\theta,\quad y = -\ell\cos\theta;\qquad \theta_{\mathrm{pol}} = \theta - \tfrac{\pi}{2}}$$

Units: $x$, $y$, $\ell$ in $\mathrm m$; angles in $\mathrm{rad}$

Meaning: measuring the angle from the downward vertical instead of from $Ox$ swaps the roles of sine and cosine and brings a minus sign into the vertical coordinate: the bob is below $O$ while $\lvert\theta\rvert < \pi/2$. The two angles grow together, so their rates are equal.

Figure 13. Polar basis of the pendulum seen with $\mathbf k$ out of the paper: $\mathbf e_R$ makes the angle $\theta$ with $-\mathbf j$, which puts the minus sign in entry $(2,1)$ of $[{}_0R_{\mathrm{pol}}]$..
Polar basis of the pendulum and its change of basis matrix Law: cylindrical local basis at the polar angle; change of basis matrix with the local unit vectors as columns; determinant; orthogonality; right-handedness Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.24; Notes.pdf, Sec. 2.6.2; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.20; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.32

View along $\mathbf k$, which points out of the paper (⊙): $\mathbf e_R$ points from $O$ along the rod to the bob; the angle $\theta$ lies between $-\mathbf j$ and $\mathbf e_R$, so in the right triangle of unit hypotenuse $\mathbf e_R$ its leg along $-\mathbf j$ (adjacent) is $\cos\theta$, which is the minus sign of the $\mathbf j$ component, and its leg along $\mathbf i$ (opposite) is $\sin\theta$. $\mathbf e_\theta$ is $\mathbf e_R$ turned a quarter turn counterclockwise, the sense in which $\theta$ grows by the right-hand rule about $\mathbf k$; the same angle $\theta$ lies between $\mathbf i$ and $\mathbf e_\theta$, so its leg along $\mathbf i$ (adjacent) is $\cos\theta$ and its leg along $\mathbf j$ (opposite) is $\sin\theta$, both positive for $\theta$ between $0$ and $\pi/2$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf e_R &= \cos\theta_{\mathrm{pol}}\,\mathbf i + \sin\theta_{\mathrm{pol}}\,\mathbf j \quad &\text{(Eq. 2.24 at the polar angle)} \\ &= \sin\theta\,\mathbf i - \cos\theta\,\mathbf j \quad &\text{(box above: the cosine and the sine of $\theta - \pi/2$)} \\ \mathbf e_\theta &= -\sin\theta_{\mathrm{pol}}\,\mathbf i + \cos\theta_{\mathrm{pol}}\,\mathbf j \quad &\text{(Eq. 2.24)} \\ &= \cos\theta\,\mathbf i + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j \quad &\text{(the same substitution: $-\sin(\theta - \pi/2) = \cos\theta$)} \\ [{}_0R_{\mathrm{pol}}] &= \begin{pmatrix} \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \cr -\cos\theta & \sin\theta & 0 \cr 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \quad &\text{(columns: $\mathbf e_R$, $\mathbf e_\theta$, $\mathbf k$ in $\mathcal B_0$, Eq. 1.13)} \\ &= [{}_0R_1(z,\theta_{\mathrm{pol}})] \quad &\text{(Eq. 1.20: a simple rotation about $\mathbf k$ by $\theta - \pi/2$)} \\ \det[{}_0R_{\mathrm{pol}}] &= 1\cdot\left(\sin\theta\sin\theta - \cos\theta\,(-\cos\theta)\right) \quad &\text{(expand along the third row)} \\ &= \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta \quad &\text{(simplify the signs)} \\ &= 1 \quad &\text{(Pythagoras)} \\ \left([{}_0R_{\mathrm{pol}}][{}_0R_{\mathrm{pol}}]^T\right)_{11} &= \sin\theta\sin\theta + \cos\theta\cos\theta + 0\cdot 0 \quad &\text{(row 1 times row 1)} \\ &= 1 \quad &\text{(Pythagoras)} \\ \left([{}_0R_{\mathrm{pol}}][{}_0R_{\mathrm{pol}}]^T\right)_{12} &= \sin\theta\,(-\cos\theta) + \cos\theta\sin\theta + 0\cdot 0 \quad &\text{(row 1 times row 2)} \\ &= 0 \quad &\text{(the two products cancel)} \\ \mathbf e_R\times\mathbf e_\theta &= \sin\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf i\times\mathbf i + \sin^2\theta\,\mathbf i\times\mathbf j - \cos^2\theta\,\mathbf j\times\mathbf i - \cos\theta\sin\theta\,\mathbf j\times\mathbf j \quad &\text{(distribute, Eq. 1.32)} \\ &= \sin^2\theta\,\mathbf i\times\mathbf j - \cos^2\theta\,\mathbf j\times\mathbf i \quad &\text{($\mathbf i\times\mathbf i = \mathbf j\times\mathbf j = \mathbf 0$)} \\ &= \sin^2\theta\,\mathbf k + \cos^2\theta\,\mathbf k \quad &\text{($\mathbf i\times\mathbf j = \mathbf k$, $\mathbf j\times\mathbf i = -\mathbf k$)} \\ &= \mathbf k \quad &\text{(Pythagoras)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf e_R = \sin\theta\,\mathbf i - \cos\theta\,\mathbf j,\qquad \mathbf e_\theta = \cos\theta\,\mathbf i + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j;\qquad [{}_0R_{\mathrm{pol}}] = \begin{bmatrix} \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ -\cos\theta & \sin\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix},\ \ \det = 1}$$

Units: dimensionless

Meaning: the remaining entries of $[{}_0R_{\mathrm{pol}}][{}_0R_{\mathrm{pol}}]^T$ follow the same way ($(2,2)$ by Pythagoras, $(1,3)$ and $(2,3)$ zero), so the polar basis is orthonormal, and with $\mathbf e_R\times\mathbf e_\theta$ equal to $\mathbf k$ it is right-handed. At $\theta = 0$ it reduces to $\mathbf e_R$ along $-\mathbf j$ and $\mathbf e_\theta$ along $\mathbf i$.

Time derivatives of the polar unit vectors Law: partial derivatives with respect to $\theta$; chain rule through $\theta(t)$; check with an angular velocity about $\mathbf k$ Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.25; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.26; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.32

The derivatives are taken in $S_0$, where $\mathbf i$, $\mathbf j$, $\mathbf k$ are constant; the polar vectors depend on time only through $\theta(t)$.

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial\mathbf e_R}{\partial\theta} &= \cos\theta\,\mathbf i + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j \quad &\text{(derivatives of $\sin\theta$ and $-\cos\theta$)} \\ &= \mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(box above)} \\ \frac{\partial\mathbf e_\theta}{\partial\theta} &= -\sin\theta\,\mathbf i + \cos\theta\,\mathbf j \quad &\text{(derivatives of $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$)} \\ &= -\mathbf e_R \quad &\text{(box above)} \\ \frac{d\mathbf e_R}{dt} &= \frac{\partial\mathbf e_R}{\partial\theta}\,\dot\theta \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ &= \dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(first result)} \\ \frac{d\mathbf e_\theta}{dt} &= \frac{\partial\mathbf e_\theta}{\partial\theta}\,\dot\theta \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ &= -\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_R \quad &\text{(second result)} \\ \dot\theta\,\mathbf k\times\mathbf e_R &= \dot\theta\left(\sin\theta\,\mathbf k\times\mathbf i - \cos\theta\,\mathbf k\times\mathbf j\right) \quad &\text{(distribute, Eq. 1.32)} \\ &= \dot\theta\left(\sin\theta\,\mathbf j + \cos\theta\,\mathbf i\right) \quad &\text{($\mathbf k\times\mathbf i = \mathbf j$, $\mathbf k\times\mathbf j = -\mathbf i$)} \\ &= \dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(the same as the derivative of $\mathbf e_R$: Eq. 1.62 with the angular velocity $\dot\theta\,\mathbf k$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\frac{d\mathbf e_R}{dt} = \dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta,\qquad \frac{d\mathbf e_\theta}{dt} = -\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_R}$$

Units: $\mathrm{rad/s}$ in every term

Meaning: the basis turns with the rod about $\mathbf k$ at the rate $\dot\theta$, the rate of $\theta_{\mathrm{pol}}$ too, so these are Eqs. 2.25 and 2.26 unchanged by the shift of the origin of the angle.

Position, velocity and acceleration of the bob Law: position along the rod; definition of velocity and acceleration; product rule; the rod length is constant Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.33; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.34; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.35; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.4; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.64
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf r_0^P &= \ell\,\mathbf e_R \quad &\text{(the bob is at distance $\ell$ from $O$ along the rod, Eq. 4.33)} \\ \mathbf v_0^P &= \left.\frac{d}{dt}\left(\ell\,\mathbf e_R\right)\right|_0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 2.3)} \\ &= \dot\ell\,\mathbf e_R + \ell\,\frac{d\mathbf e_R}{dt} \quad &\text{(product rule, Eq. 1.64)} \\ &= \ell\,\frac{d\mathbf e_R}{dt} \quad &\text{(rigid rod: $\dot\ell = 0$)} \\ &= \ell\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(box above; Eq. 4.34)} \\ \mathbf a_0^P &= \left.\frac{d}{dt}\left(\ell\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta\right)\right|_0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 2.4)} \\ &= \ell\ddot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta + \ell\dot\theta\,\frac{d\mathbf e_\theta}{dt} \quad &\text{(product rule; $\ell$ constant)} \\ &= \ell\ddot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta - \ell\dot\theta^2\,\mathbf e_R \quad &\text{(box above)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_0^P = \ell\,\mathbf e_R,\qquad \mathbf v_0^P = \ell\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta,\qquad \mathbf a_0^P = -\ell\dot\theta^2\,\mathbf e_R + \ell\ddot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta}$$

Units: $\mathrm m$; $\mathrm m\cdot\mathrm{rad/s} = \mathrm{m/s}$; $\mathrm m\cdot\mathrm{rad^2/s^2}$ and $\mathrm m\cdot\mathrm{rad/s^2}$, both $\mathrm{m/s^2}$

Meaning: the velocity is perpendicular to the rod, tangent to the circle of radius $\ell$; the acceleration has a part along the rod pointing to $O$, which turns the velocity, and a part along $\mathbf e_\theta$, which changes the speed.

Forces and equations of motion

The bob is subject to two forces (Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.7): the constant weight, pointing downwards, and the tension of the rod, a reaction force (Topic 3) whose magnitude $F_t$ is unknown until the problem is solved but whose direction is along the rod. The rod is light and rigid, so the force it exerts on the bob acts along $\mathbf e_R$; with $F_t$ positive it pulls the bob towards $O$.

Figure 14. Forces on the bob: weight $m g\cos\theta\,\mathbf e_R - m g\sin\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta$ and tension $-F_t\,\mathbf e_R$, perpendicular to the velocity (Notes.pdf Eq. 4.36)..
The forces in the polar basis Law: change of basis with the transpose of the rotation matrix; tension along the rod Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.36; Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.7; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.12; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.14
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf F_g &= -m\,g\,\mathbf j \quad &\text{(weight, downwards)} \\ [\mathbf F_g]_{\mathrm{pol}} &= [{}_0R_{\mathrm{pol}}]^T\,[\mathbf F_g]_0 \quad &\text{(inverse change of basis: the transpose, Eqs. 1.12 and 1.14)} \\ &= \begin{pmatrix} \sin\theta\cdot 0 + (-\cos\theta)(-m g) + 0\cdot 0 \cr \cos\theta\cdot 0 + \sin\theta\,(-m g) + 0\cdot 0 \cr 0\cdot 0 + 0\cdot(-m g) + 1\cdot 0 \end{pmatrix} \quad &\text{(rows of the transpose, the columns of the matrix, times the column $(0, -mg, 0)$)} \\ &= \begin{pmatrix} m g\cos\theta \cr -m g\sin\theta \cr 0 \end{pmatrix} \quad &\text{(arithmetic)} \\ \mathbf F_t &= -F_t\,\mathbf e_R \quad &\text{(tension along the rod, towards $O$ for $F_t > 0$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf F_g = m g\cos\theta\,\mathbf e_R - m g\sin\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta,\qquad \mathbf F_t = -F_t\,\mathbf e_R}$$

Units: $\mathrm N$

Meaning: the component of the weight along the rod, $m g\cos\theta$, points away from $O$ while the bob is below the pivot; the component along $\mathbf e_\theta$, $-m g\sin\theta$, points back towards $\theta = 0$ whenever $\lvert\theta\rvert < \pi$: it is a restoring force that tries to bring the pendulum back to its equilibrium position (Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.7).

Equations of motion of the pendulum Law: Newton's second law projected on $\mathbf e_R$ and $\mathbf e_\theta$ Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.37; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.38; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.4; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.35; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.36
$$\begin{aligned} m\,\mathbf a_0^P &= \mathbf F_g + \mathbf F_t \quad &\text{(second law, Eq. 4.4)} \\ m\left(-\ell\dot\theta^2\,\mathbf e_R + \ell\ddot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta\right) &= m g\cos\theta\,\mathbf e_R - m g\sin\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta - F_t\,\mathbf e_R \quad &\text{(substitute the acceleration, Eq. 4.35, the weight, Eq. 4.36, and the force of the rod, previous box)} \\ &= \left(m g\cos\theta - F_t\right)\mathbf e_R - m g\sin\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(group the terms by unit vector)} \\ \mathbf e_R:\quad -m\ell\dot\theta^2 &= m g\cos\theta - F_t \quad &\text{(dot-multiply by $\mathbf e_R$)} \\ \mathbf e_\theta:\quad m\ell\ddot\theta &= -m g\sin\theta \quad &\text{(dot-multiply by $\mathbf e_\theta$)} \\ \ddot\theta + \frac{g}{\ell}\sin\theta &= 0 \quad &\text{(divide by $m\ell$ and move the right side over)} \\ F_t &= m\ell\dot\theta^2 + m g\cos\theta \quad &\text{(solve the $\mathbf e_R$ equation for the tension)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\ddot\theta + \frac{g}{\ell}\sin\theta = 0,\qquad F_t = m\ell\dot\theta^2 + m g\cos\theta}$$

Units: $\mathrm{rad/s^2}$ in the equation of motion ($g/\ell$ in $\mathrm{s^{-2}}$); $\mathrm N$ in the tension ($\mathrm{kg\cdot m\cdot s^{-2}}$ for both terms)

Meaning: the $\mathbf e_\theta$ equation contains only the unknown $\theta$ and is the equation of motion; the mass drops out of it. The $\mathbf e_R$ equation then gives the tension: at the lowest point it is the weight plus the force $m\ell\dot\theta^2$ needed to turn the velocity.

Erratum to Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.37: sign of the tension

Eq. 4.37 is printed with $+F_t$ on its right side, but the notes define the tension as $-F_t\,\mathbf e_R$, whose component along $\mathbf e_R$ is $-F_t$, so the projection on $\mathbf e_R$ is the one of the box above, with $-F_t$ on the right. Check: for the pendulum hanging at rest at its lowest point the printed equation would give a tension equal to $-mg$, a rod pushing the bob downwards, while the corrected one gives $mg$, the rod holding the weight. The error does not affect Eq. 4.38 or anything else in the section.

Energy

First integral of the equation of motion Law: multiplication by $\dot\theta$; chain rule; integration in time with Barrow's rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.39; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.38
$$\begin{aligned} \dot\theta\,\ddot\theta + \frac{g}{\ell}\sin\theta\,\dot\theta &= 0 \quad &\text{(multiply Eq. 4.38 by $\dot\theta$)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\tfrac12\,\dot\theta^2\right) &= \dot\theta\,\ddot\theta \quad &\text{(chain rule: derivative of the square times the derivative of $\dot\theta$)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{g}{\ell}\left(1 - \cos\theta\right)\right) &= \frac{g}{\ell}\sin\theta\,\dot\theta \quad &\text{(chain rule: derivative of $-\cos\theta$ times $\dot\theta$)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\tfrac12\,\dot\theta^2 + \frac{g}{\ell}\left(1 - \cos\theta\right)\right) &= 0 \quad &\text{(the first row is the sum of the two derivatives)} \\ \left[\tfrac12\,\dot\theta^2 + \frac{g}{\ell}\left(1 - \cos\theta\right)\right]_{0}^{t} &= 0 \quad &\text{(integrate from $0$ to $t$; Barrow)} \\ \tfrac12\,\dot\theta^2 + \frac{g}{\ell}\left(1 - \cos\theta\right) &= C \quad &\text{($C$: the value of the bracket at $t = 0$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\tfrac12\,\dot\theta^2 + \frac{g}{\ell}\left(1 - \cos\theta\right) = C}$$

Units: $\mathrm{rad^2/s^2}$, that is $\mathrm{s^{-2}}$, in every term and in $C$

Meaning: a first integral: a combination of $\theta$ and $\dot\theta$ that stays constant during the motion. The mass does not appear in it (Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.7).

The same result follows directly from energy conservation (Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.7): the tension exerts no work on the bob, being always perpendicular to its velocity, and the weight is uniform and derives from a potential. From Section 8 on, the indices $P$ and $0$ of the energies are dropped where no confusion arises, since there is one particle and one frame.

Potential, kinetic and mechanical energy of the pendulum Law: potential energy of the weight (Section 4); zero power of a force perpendicular to the velocity; kinetic energy Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.40; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.41; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.42; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.10; [Lecture 2, Slide 16]; [Lecture 2, Slide 19]
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf F_t\cdot\mathbf v_0^P &= -F_t\,\mathbf e_R\cdot\ell\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(tension and Eq. 4.34)} \\ &= 0 \quad &\text{($\mathbf e_R\cdot\mathbf e_\theta = 0$: the tension does no work)} \\ V_0 &= m g\,y + \mathrm{const} \quad &\text{(potential energy of the weight, Section 4, with any reference level)} \\ &= m g\,(y + \ell) \quad &\text{(zero at the lowest point, $y = -\ell$)} \\ &= m g\ell\left(1 - \cos\theta\right) \quad &\text{(previous box: $y = -\ell\cos\theta$; Eq. 4.40)} \\ T_0 &= \tfrac12\,m\,\ell\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta\cdot\ell\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.2 with Eq. 4.34)} \\ &= \tfrac12\,m\left(\ell\dot\theta\right)^2 \quad &\text{($\mathbf e_\theta\cdot\mathbf e_\theta = 1$; Eq. 4.41)} \\ E_0 &= \tfrac12\,m\left(\ell\dot\theta\right)^2 + m g\ell\left(1 - \cos\theta\right) \quad &\text{(the only working force is conservative: $E_0$ is constant, Eq. 4.42)} \\ &= m\ell^2\left(\tfrac12\,\dot\theta^2 + \frac{g}{\ell}\left(1 - \cos\theta\right)\right) \quad &\text{(take out the factor $m\ell^2$)} \\ &= m\ell^2\,C \quad &\text{(first integral, Eq. 4.39)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{V_0(\theta) = m g\ell\left(1 - \cos\theta\right),\qquad T_0 = \tfrac12\,m\left(\ell\dot\theta\right)^2,\qquad T_0 + V_0 = E_0 = m\ell^2\,C}$$

Units: $\mathrm J$; $\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$ times $C$ in $\mathrm{s^{-2}}$ is also $\mathrm J$

Meaning: the conservation of energy is Eq. 4.39 multiplied by the constant factor $m\ell^2$ (Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.7). In general the energy equation, when available, can replace one of the scalar equations of motion, of which it is a combination; it is especially useful in problems with a single degree of freedom.

Figure 15. Potential energy of the simple pendulum $V_0(\theta) = m g\ell(1 - \cos\theta)$ and, dashed, that of the linearised problem $\tilde V_0(\theta) = m g\ell\,\theta^2/2$; $E_{0,1}$ gives an oscillation between $\pm\theta^*$, $E_{0,2}$ a rotation (Notes.pdf Fig. 4.4)..
Equilibria of the pendulum and their stability Law: equation of motion written with the potential; critical points and second derivative of the potential (Section 6) Source: Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.6; Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.7; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.40; Notes.pdf Fig. 4.4; [Lecture 2, Slide 22]

$n$ is any integer.

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{dV_0}{d\theta} &= m g\ell\sin\theta \quad &\text{(derivative of Eq. 4.40)} \\ m\ell^2\,\ddot\theta &= -\frac{dV_0}{d\theta} \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.38 times $m\ell^2$: the form of Eq. 4.21 with $\theta$ for $x$ and $m\ell^2$ for $m$)} \\ \sin\theta^*_{\mathrm{eq}} &= 0 \quad &\text{(equilibrium: critical point of $V_0$)} \\ \theta^*_{\mathrm{eq}} &= n\pi \quad &\text{(zeros of the sine)} \\ \frac{d^2V_0}{d\theta^2} &= m g\ell\cos\theta \quad &\text{(second derivative)} \\ \frac{d^2V_0}{d\theta^2}(2n\pi) &= m g\ell > 0 \quad &\text{(hanging down: a minimum)} \\ \frac{d^2V_0}{d\theta^2}(\pi + 2n\pi) &= -m g\ell < 0 \quad &\text{(upside down: a maximum)} \\ m\ell^2 p^2 + m g\ell\cos\theta^*_{\mathrm{eq}} &= 0 \quad &\text{(characteristic equation of Section 6 with $m\ell^2$ for $m$)} \\ p &= \pm\,i\sqrt{g/\ell} \quad &\text{(at $\theta^*_{\mathrm{eq}} = 2n\pi$: $\cos\theta^*_{\mathrm{eq}} = 1$, divide by $m\ell^2$)} \\ p &= \pm\sqrt{g/\ell} \quad &\text{(at $\theta^*_{\mathrm{eq}} = \pi + 2n\pi$: $\cos\theta^*_{\mathrm{eq}} = -1$)} \\ V_0(\pi + 2n\pi) &= m g\ell\left(1 - (-1)\right) \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.40 at the maxima)} \\ &= 2\,m g\ell \quad &\text{(arithmetic)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\theta^*_{\mathrm{eq}} = 2n\pi \ \text{stable (minima, } V_0 = 0\text{)},\qquad \theta^*_{\mathrm{eq}} = \pi + 2n\pi \ \text{unstable (maxima, } V_0 = 2\,m g\ell\text{)}}$$

Units: $\mathrm{J/rad}$ and $\mathrm{J/rad^2}$ for the derivatives of $V_0$; $p$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$

Meaning: the minima and maxima of Fig. 4.4 (Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.7): the hanging pendulum oscillates after a small push, and the inverted one falls away at an exponential rate. By the boxes of Section 6, every small perturbation of the inverted pendulum except a finely tuned one grows.

Classes of motion

Let the bob start at its equilibrium position, the lowest point, with the speed $v_{0,0}^P$ towards the right, and ask which motions are possible for each value of that speed (Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.7). Since the potential is zero there, the mechanical energy is the initial kinetic energy.

Oscillations: the turning points Law: conservation of mechanical energy; the kinetic energy vanishes at a turning point Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.43; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.42; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.40
$$\begin{aligned} E_0 &= \tfrac12\,m\left(v_{0,0}^P\right)^2 + V_0(0) \quad &\text{(initial state: speed $v_{0,0}^P$ at $\theta = 0$)} \\ &= \tfrac12\,m\left(v_{0,0}^P\right)^2 \quad &\text{($V_0(0) = m g\ell(1 - 1) = 0$)} \\ V_0(\theta^*) &= E_0 \quad &\text{(turning point: $T_0 = 0$, which needs $E_0 < 2\,m g\ell$)} \\ m g\ell\left(1 - \cos\theta^*\right) &= \tfrac12\,m\left(v_{0,0}^P\right)^2 \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.40 and the second row)} \\ 1 - \cos\theta^* &= \frac{\left(v_{0,0}^P\right)^2}{2 g\ell} \quad &\text{(divide by $m g\ell$)} \\ \cos\theta^* &= 1 - \frac{\left(v_{0,0}^P\right)^2}{2 g\ell} \quad &\text{(rearrange)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\cos\theta^* = 1 - \frac{\left(v_{0,0}^P\right)^2}{2 g\ell}}$$

Units: $(\mathrm{m/s})^2/(\mathrm{m/s^2}\cdot\mathrm m)$, dimensionless

Meaning: if $E_0$ is below $2\,m g\ell$ (the level $E_{0,1}$ of Fig. 4.4) the motion is confined between the two angles $\pm\theta^*$, the turning points where the kinetic energy vanishes and the bob stops for an instant before turning back: an oscillation of amplitude $\theta^*$. The right side lies between $-1$ and $1$ exactly when the starting speed squared is below $4 g\ell$, which is the same condition, $E_0$ below $2\,m g\ell$.

Period of the oscillations Law: energy equation solved for the rate; change of the integration variable from time to angle; symmetry of the two halves of the cycle Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.44; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.42

In the half cycle from $-\theta^*$ to $\theta^*$, from the instant $-t^*$ to $t^*$, the rate $\dot\theta$ is positive; in the other half it is negative.

$$\begin{aligned} \tfrac12\,m\ell^2\dot\theta^2 &= E_0 - V_0(\theta) \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.42 with $T_0 = \tfrac12\,m\ell^2\dot\theta^2$)} \\ \left\lvert\frac{d\theta}{dt}\right\rvert &= \sqrt{\frac{2E_0 - 2V_0(\theta)}{m\ell^2}} \quad &\text{(solve for the magnitude of the rate)} \\ \tau &= 2\int_{-t^*}^{t^*}dt \quad &\text{(the return half takes the same time: $\lvert\dot\theta\rvert$ depends only on $\theta$)} \\ &= 2\int_{-\theta^*}^{\theta^*}\frac{d\theta}{d\theta/dt} \quad &\text{(change of variable $t \to \theta$: differential $d\theta = \dot\theta\,dt$, limits $-\theta^*$ and $\theta^*$)} \\ &= 2\int_{-\theta^*}^{\theta^*}\sqrt{\frac{m\ell^2}{2E_0 - 2V_0(\theta)}}\,d\theta \quad &\text{(second row, with $\dot\theta > 0$ in this half)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\tau = 2\int_{-t^*}^{t^*}dt = 2\int_{-\theta^*}^{\theta^*}\sqrt{\frac{m\ell^2}{2E_0 - 2V_0(\theta)}}\,d\theta}$$

Units: $\sqrt{\mathrm{kg\,m^2}/\mathrm J} = \mathrm s$ for the integrand per radian, so $\tau$ is in $\mathrm s$

Meaning: the period depends on the amplitude through $E_0$. The integrand grows without bound at the turning points, where the bob stops, but the integral is finite (next box; the box on small oscillations below evaluates it in that limit).

The period integral is finite Law: potential energy of the pendulum; first-order Taylor expansion of the cosine about the turning point; antiderivative of a power; Barrow's rule with a moving limit Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.40; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.44

The amplitude lies between $0$ and $\pi$, so the sine of $\theta^*$ is positive. $\theta_a$ is a fixed angle a little below $\theta^*$ and $\theta_b$ an upper limit that tends to $\theta^*$ from below; at the turning point the kinetic energy vanishes, so $E_0$ equals the potential energy at $\theta^*$.

$$\begin{aligned} 2E_0 - 2V_0(\theta) &= 2\,m g\ell\left(1 - \cos\theta^*\right) - 2\,m g\ell\left(1 - \cos\theta\right) \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.40 at $\theta^*$ and at $\theta$)} \\ &= 2\,m g\ell\left(\cos\theta - \cos\theta^*\right) \quad &\text{(the terms $2\,m g\ell$ cancel)} \\ \cos\theta &= \cos\theta^* - \sin\theta^*\left(\theta - \theta^*\right) + O\big((\theta - \theta^*)^2\big) \quad &\text{(first-order Taylor expansion of the cosine about $\theta^*$; its derivative is minus the sine)} \\ 2E_0 - 2V_0(\theta) &\simeq 2\,m g\ell\sin\theta^*\left(\theta^* - \theta\right) \quad &\text{(substitute in the second row, near $\theta^*$)} \\ \sqrt{\frac{m\ell^2}{2E_0 - 2V_0(\theta)}} &\simeq \sqrt{\frac{\ell}{2 g\sin\theta^*}}\left(\theta^* - \theta\right)^{-1/2} \quad &\text{(the integrand of the previous box; $m\ell^2/(2\,m g\ell)$ simplifies to $\ell/(2g)$)} \\ \frac{d}{d\theta}\left[-2\left(\theta^* - \theta\right)^{1/2}\right] &= -2\cdot\tfrac12\left(\theta^* - \theta\right)^{-1/2}\cdot(-1) \quad &\text{(chain rule: the derivative of $\theta^* - \theta$ is $-1$)} \\ &= \left(\theta^* - \theta\right)^{-1/2} \quad &\text{(arithmetic: an antiderivative of the power)} \\ \int_{\theta_a}^{\theta_b}\left(\theta^* - \theta\right)^{-1/2}d\theta &= \Big[-2\left(\theta^* - \theta\right)^{1/2}\Big]_{\theta_a}^{\theta_b} \quad &\text{(the antiderivative of the two rows above)} \\ &= -2\left(\theta^* - \theta_b\right)^{1/2} + 2\left(\theta^* - \theta_a\right)^{1/2} \quad &\text{(Barrow: upper limit minus lower limit)} \\ &\to 2\left(\theta^* - \theta_a\right)^{1/2} \quad &\text{(limit $\theta_b \to \theta^*$: the first term tends to zero)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\sqrt{\frac{m\ell^2}{2E_0 - 2V_0(\theta)}} \simeq \sqrt{\frac{\ell}{2 g\sin\theta^*}}\left(\theta^* - \theta\right)^{-1/2},\qquad \int_{\theta_a}^{\theta^*}\left(\theta^* - \theta\right)^{-1/2}d\theta = 2\left(\theta^* - \theta_a\right)^{1/2} \ \text{(finite)}}$$

Units: $\sqrt{\mathrm m/(\mathrm{m/s^2})} = \mathrm s$ for the factor of the integrand; the angles in radians

Meaning: near the turning point the integrand of the period is a constant times an inverse square root of the distance to $\theta^*$, and the integral of that inverse square root has a finite limit, so the contribution of the end of the interval to the period is finite; the end at $-\theta^*$ is the same by the symmetry of the potential, and between the two ends the integrand is bounded. The period is therefore finite for every amplitude below $\pi$.

Rotations: energy above the maxima Law: conservation of mechanical energy; the potential never exceeds its maximum Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.45; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.40; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.42
$$\begin{aligned} V_0(\theta) &\leq 2\,m g\ell \quad &\text{($1 - \cos\theta \leq 2$ for every $\theta$)} \\ T_0 &= E_0 - V_0(\theta) \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.42)} \\ &\geq E_0 - 2\,m g\ell > 0 \quad &\text{(first row, with $E_0 > 2\,m g\ell$)} \\ T_{0,\mathrm{up}} &= \tfrac12\,m\left(v_{0,\mathrm{up}}^P\right)^2 \quad &\text{(at the upward vertical, $\theta = \pi$, where the speed is $v_{0,\mathrm{up}}^P$)} \\ &= E_0 - 2\,m g\ell \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.42 with $V_0(\pi) = 2\,m g\ell$; Eq. 4.45)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{T_{0,\mathrm{up}} = \tfrac12\,m\left(v_{0,\mathrm{up}}^P\right)^2 = E_0 - 2\,m g\ell > 0}$$

Units: $\mathrm J$

Meaning: if the bob is pushed so hard that $E_0$ exceeds $2\,m g\ell$ (the level $E_{0,2}$ of Fig. 4.4) the kinetic energy never vanishes, the rate keeps its sign, and the bob passes the upward vertical with a nonzero speed: the motion is a continuous rotation rather than an oscillation (Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.7).

Small oscillations

If the mechanical energy is small compared with $2\,m g\ell$, the oscillations are small and the angle stays much smaller than one radian; the equation of motion can then be linearised, giving an approximate but simpler model of the pendulum (Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.7).

Linearised pendulum and its potential Law: Taylor expansions of the sine and the cosine about zero, kept to the lowest order Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.46; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.47; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.38; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.40; Notes.pdf Fig. 4.4
$$\begin{aligned} \sin\theta &= \theta - \frac{\theta^3}{6} + O(\theta^5) \quad &\text{(Taylor series of the sine)} \\ \sin\theta &\approx \theta \quad &\text{(keep the first-order term, $\theta$ much smaller than one)} \\ \ddot\theta + \frac{g}{\ell}\,\theta &= 0 \quad &\text{(substitute in Eq. 4.38; Eq. 4.46)} \\ 1 - \cos\theta &= \frac{\theta^2}{2} - \frac{\theta^4}{24} + O(\theta^6) \quad &\text{(Taylor series of the cosine)} \\ \tilde V_0(\theta) &= m g\ell\,\frac{\theta^2}{2} \quad &\text{(keep the lowest-order term in Eq. 4.40; Eq. 4.47)} \\ -\frac{d\tilde V_0}{d\theta} &= -m g\ell\,\theta \quad &\text{(derivative of $\tilde V_0$)} \\ &= m\ell^2\,\ddot\theta \quad &\text{(the linearised equation times $m\ell^2$: the same model)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\ddot\theta + \frac{g}{\ell}\,\theta = 0,\qquad \tilde V_0(\theta) = m g\ell\,\frac{\theta^2}{2}}$$

Units: $\mathrm{s^{-2}}$ in the equation; $\mathrm J$ for the potential

Meaning: the equation of a harmonic oscillator (Chapter 5); its potential is the parabola drawn dashed in Fig. 4.4, which matches the full potential near the bottom and departs from it as the amplitude grows. At an amplitude of $10^\circ$, about $0.1745\ \mathrm{rad}$, the sine is $0.1736$, so replacing it by the angle overestimates the restoring force by about $0.5\ \%$.

Period of the small oscillations Law: period integral with the linearised potential; trigonometric substitution; Barrow's rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.44; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.47

At the turning point the energy is all potential, so with the linearised potential the energy is $m g\ell$ times half the amplitude squared.

$$\begin{aligned} E_0 &= m g\ell\,\frac{\theta^{*2}}{2} \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.47 at $\theta^*$, where $T_0 = 0$)} \\ 2E_0 - 2\tilde V_0(\theta) &= m g\ell\left(\theta^{*2} - \theta^2\right) \quad &\text{(subtract twice Eq. 4.47)} \\ \sqrt{\frac{m\ell^2}{2E_0 - 2\tilde V_0}} &= \sqrt{\frac{\ell}{g}}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{\theta^{*2} - \theta^2}} \quad &\text{(cancel $m\ell$)} \\ \tau &= 2\sqrt{\frac{\ell}{g}}\int_{-\theta^*}^{\theta^*}\frac{d\theta}{\sqrt{\theta^{*2} - \theta^2}} \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.44)} \\ \theta &= \theta^*\sin u,\qquad d\theta = \theta^*\cos u\,du \quad &\text{(substitution and its differential)} \\ \sqrt{\theta^{*2} - \theta^{*2}\sin^2 u} &= \theta^*\cos u \quad &\text{(Pythagoras; $\cos u \geq 0$ for $u$ between $-\pi/2$ and $\pi/2$)} \\ \tau &= 2\sqrt{\frac{\ell}{g}}\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\frac{\theta^*\cos u}{\theta^*\cos u}\,du \quad &\text{(limits: $\theta = -\theta^*$ gives $u = -\pi/2$, $\theta = \theta^*$ gives $u = \pi/2$)} \\ &= 2\sqrt{\frac{\ell}{g}}\,\big[u\big]_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \quad &\text{(the integrand is one; antiderivative $u$)} \\ &= 2\sqrt{\frac{\ell}{g}}\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\right) \quad &\text{(Barrow)} \\ &= 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\ell}{g}} \quad &\text{(arithmetic)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\tau = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\ell}{g}}}$$

Units: $\sqrt{\mathrm m/(\mathrm{m/s^2})} = \mathrm s$

Meaning: for small oscillations the period does not depend on the amplitude or on the mass; it is $2\pi$ over the imaginary part $\sqrt{g/\ell}$ of the characteristic roots found at $\theta = 0$, as the harmonic oscillator of Chapter 5 will confirm. For a rod of $1\ \mathrm m$ and $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ it is about $2.01\ \mathrm s$.

8. The harmonic oscillator: undamped motion

From the classical spring-mass-damper system to the linearised aeroelastic oscillations of an airfoil or the vibrations of an aircraft structure, many mechanical systems have an equation of motion that reduces to a linear second-order equation with constant coefficients in a generalised coordinate $\xi$, with two constants $\gamma$ and $\omega_0$ and a forcing term $\tilde f(t)$: this is the most general expression of the equation of a harmonic oscillator (Notes.pdf, Ch. 5), and any physical system governed by such an equation is termed a harmonic oscillator ([Lecture 6, Slide 5]). Since a single particle is studied in the single frame $S_0$, the indices $P$ and $0$ of the previous sections are dropped for many quantities: the displacement is $x$, the potential energy $V$, the mechanical energy $E$ (Notes.pdf, Ch. 5). The sections that follow take Chapter 5 of the notes in its order (Eqs. 5.1 to 5.47) with the slides of Lecture 6 at the places where they treat the same material, and close with the linearisation about an equilibrium of [Lecture 6, Slide 15] and an extended example.

The spring-mass-damper system ([Lecture 6, Slide 5]; Notes.pdf, Sec. 5.1)

Example

A point particle $P$ of mass $m$ moves along the horizontal line $Ox$ of the inertial frame $S_0$, on a smooth support. It is attached to the wall at $O$ by a linear spring of stiffness $k$ and zero natural length and by a viscous damper of damping constant $\lambda$, and an external force $F_x(t)$ may be applied to it along $Ox$. Its weight and the reaction of the support are vertical. The undamped oscillator of this section is the case of no damper and no applied force; the damper is added in Section 10 and the applied force in Section 11.

DataValue
frame$S_0$, inertial; $\mathbf i$ along the line of motion, away from the wall; $\mathbf j$ vertical upwards
particlemass $m$, position $x$ along $Ox$ (the length of the spring)
springstiffness $k > 0$, zero natural length
damperdamping constant $\lambda \geq 0$
applied force$F_x(t)$ along $\mathbf i$
Figure 16. Spring-mass-damper system and the forces on the mass: $-k x\,\mathbf i$, $-\lambda\dot x\,\mathbf i$ and $F_x(t)\,\mathbf i$ along the line of motion; the weight and the reaction of the floor cancel ([Lecture 6, Slide 5])..
Equation of motion of the spring-mass-damper Law: Newton's second law projected on the line of motion; linear spring and viscous damper Source: [Lecture 6, Slide 5]; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.1; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.19; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.20; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.32; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.23; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.4

The spring has zero natural length, so its elongation is the displacement $x$ itself; the damper opposes the velocity. $\mathbf N_s$ is the reaction of the smooth support, vertical.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf r_0^P &= x\,\mathbf i \quad &\text{(the particle moves on $Ox$)} \\ \mathbf a_0^P &= \ddot x\,\mathbf i \quad &\text{(differentiate twice in $S_0$, where $\mathbf i$ is constant, Eq. 2.4)} \\ \mathbf F_k &= -k\,x\,\mathbf i \quad &\text{(linear spring: proportional to the elongation, towards the wall; Eq. 5.1)} \\ \mathbf F_\lambda &= -\lambda\,\dot x\,\mathbf i \quad &\text{(viscous damper: proportional and opposite to the velocity)} \\ m\ddot x\,\mathbf i &= -k\,x\,\mathbf i - \lambda\dot x\,\mathbf i + F_x(t)\,\mathbf i + \left(\mathbf N_s - m g\,\mathbf j\right) \quad &\text{(second law, Eq. 4.4, with every force)} \\ \mathbf N_s &= m g\,\mathbf j \quad &\text{(component along $\mathbf j$: the left side has none)} \\ m\ddot x &= -k\,x - \lambda\dot x + F_x(t) \quad &\text{(component along $\mathbf i$)} \\ m\ddot x + \lambda\dot x + k\,x &= F_x(t) \quad &\text{(move the spring and damper terms to the left; Eq. 5.32)} \\ \ddot x + \frac{\lambda}{m}\,\dot x + \frac{k}{m}\,x &= \frac{F_x(t)}{m} \quad &\text{(divide by $m$)} \\ \ddot x + 2\gamma\,\dot x + \omega_0^2\,x &= \frac{F_x(t)}{m} \quad &\text{(name the coefficients: $\gamma = \lambda/(2m)$, $\omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m}$, Eq. 5.23)} \\ m\ddot x + k\,x &= 0 \quad &\text{(no damper and no applied force: $\lambda = 0$, $F_x = 0$; Eq. 5.4)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{m\ddot x + \lambda\dot x + k\,x = F_x(t) \ \Longleftrightarrow\ \ddot x + 2\gamma\,\dot x + \omega_0^2\,x = \frac{F_x(t)}{m},\qquad \gamma = \frac{\lambda}{2m},\ \ \omega_0 = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}}$$

Units: every term of the first form in $\mathrm N$ ($\mathrm{kg\,m/s^2}$, $\mathrm{(N\,s/m)(m/s)}$, $\mathrm{(N/m)\,m}$); $\gamma$ in $\mathrm{(N\,s/m)/kg} = \mathrm{s^{-1}}$; $\omega_0$ in $\sqrt{\mathrm{(N/m)/kg}} = \mathrm{s^{-1}}$; every term of the second form in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$

Meaning: the spring and the damper give forces linear in $x$ and $\dot x$, so the equation of motion is linear with constant coefficients: it is the general equation of a harmonic oscillator with $x$ as the coordinate and $F_x/m$ as the forcing term ([Lecture 6, Slide 5]). The weight is carried by the support and does not enter the motion. The last row, Eq. 5.4, is the undamped free oscillator studied in this section.

Potential energy of the spring and the turning points Law: potential energy of a one-dimensional force depending only on the position; conservation of mechanical energy; a turning point has zero velocity Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.1; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.2; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.26; [Lecture 6, Slide 7]

The reference position, where the potential is zero, is the relaxed spring, $x$ equal to zero; $x'$ is the integration variable.

$$\begin{aligned} V(x) &= -\int_0^x F(x')\,dx' \quad &\text{(one-dimensional potential, Eq. 4.15)} \\ &= -\int_0^x\left(-k\,x'\right)dx' \quad &\text{(spring force, Eq. 5.1)} \\ &= k\int_0^x x'\,dx' \quad &\text{(take the constant $-k$ out of the integral)} \\ &= k\left[\frac{x'^2}{2}\right]_0^x \quad &\text{(antiderivative of $x'$)} \\ &= k\left(\frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{0^2}{2}\right) \quad &\text{(Barrow)} \\ &= \tfrac12\,k\,x^2 \quad &\text{(Eq. 5.2)} \\ &= \tfrac12\,m\,\omega_0^2\,x^2 \quad &\text{($k = m\omega_0^2$, Eq. 5.23)} \\ \tfrac12\,m\,\dot x^2 + \tfrac12\,k\,x^2 &= E \quad &\text{(the only working force is conservative: $E$ is constant, Eq. 4.26)} \\ \tfrac12\,k\,x^2 &= E \quad &\text{(at a turning point $\dot x = 0$)} \\ x &= \pm\sqrt{2E/k} \quad &\text{(multiply by $2/k$ and take the square root; Eq. 5.3)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{V(x) = \tfrac12\,k\,x^2 = \tfrac12\,m\,\omega_0^2\,x^2,\qquad x = \pm a = \pm\sqrt{2E/k}}$$

Units: $\mathrm{(N/m)\,m^2} = \mathrm J$ for the potential; $\sqrt{\mathrm J/(\mathrm{N/m})} = \mathrm m$ for the turning points

Meaning: the potential is a parabola (Notes.pdf Fig. 5.1). With $k$ positive, every energy $E$ above zero meets it at exactly two points, the turning points $\pm a$, where the particle stops and turns back: the motion is a harmonic oscillation between them (Notes.pdf, Sec. 5.1). The constant $a$ is identified with the amplitude in the box on the energy of the oscillation below.

Figure 17. Potential energy of the harmonic oscillator $V(x) = \tfrac12 k x^2$; an energy $E$ allows the motion between the turning points $\pm a = \pm\sqrt{2E/k}$ (Notes.pdf Fig. 5.1; [Lecture 6, Slide 7])..
Linear homogeneous equations: superposition and the characteristic equation Law: linearity of differentiation; trial exponential solution; independence of two solutions Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.5; Notes.pdf, Sec. 5.1; [Lecture 6, Slide 3]

The equation is the homogeneous one, $\tilde f$ equal to zero, with constant coefficients $b_2$ (nonzero), $b_1$, $b_0$. $\xi_1$ and $\xi_2$ are two of its solutions and $D_1$, $D_2$ any two constants.

$$\begin{aligned} b_2\ddot\xi_1 + b_1\dot\xi_1 + b_0\xi_1 &= 0,\qquad b_2\ddot\xi_2 + b_1\dot\xi_2 + b_0\xi_2 = 0 \quad &\text{(both are solutions)} \\ \xi &= D_1\xi_1 + D_2\xi_2 \quad &\text{(a linear combination, Eq. 5.5)} \\ \dot\xi &= D_1\dot\xi_1 + D_2\dot\xi_2 \quad &\text{(derivative of a sum; the constants come out)} \\ \ddot\xi &= D_1\ddot\xi_1 + D_2\ddot\xi_2 \quad &\text{(differentiate again)} \\ b_2\ddot\xi + b_1\dot\xi + b_0\xi &= D_1\left(b_2\ddot\xi_1 + b_1\dot\xi_1 + b_0\xi_1\right) + D_2\left(b_2\ddot\xi_2 + b_1\dot\xi_2 + b_0\xi_2\right) \quad &\text{(substitute and group by constant)} \\ &= 0 \quad &\text{(first row: both brackets vanish)} \\ \xi &= \exp(p\,t) \quad &\text{(trial solution, $p$ a constant, possibly complex)} \\ \dot\xi &= p\exp(p\,t) \quad &\text{(chain rule: the derivative of $p\,t$ is $p$)} \\ \ddot\xi &= p^2\exp(p\,t) \quad &\text{(chain rule again)} \\ \left(b_2\,p^2 + b_1\,p + b_0\right)\exp(p\,t) &= 0 \quad &\text{(substitute in the homogeneous equation and take out the exponential)} \\ b_2\,p^2 + b_1\,p + b_0 &= 0 \quad &\text{(the exponential is never zero: characteristic equation)} \\ \frac{\exp(p_+ t)}{\exp(p_- t)} &= \exp\big((p_+ - p_-)\,t\big) \quad &\text{(two roots $p_+$, $p_-$: the quotient of the two solutions)} \\ \xi &= D_1\exp(p_+ t) + D_2\exp(p_- t) \quad &\text{(if $p_+ \neq p_-$ the quotient is not constant: two independent solutions, combined)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{b_2\,p^2 + b_1\,p + b_0 = 0;\qquad p_+ \neq p_-:\ \ \xi = D_1\exp(p_+ t) + D_2\exp(p_- t)}$$

Units: $p$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, so that $p\,t$ is dimensionless; $b_2\,p^2$, $b_1\,p$ and $b_0$ have the same units, those of the coefficient $b_0$

Meaning: the solutions of the homogeneous equation satisfy the superposition principle and form a two-dimensional vector space of functions: the two exponentials are a basis of it and $D_1$, $D_2$ are the components of a solution in that basis ([Lecture 6, Slide 3]). A second-order equation has exactly two arbitrary constants, so this is the general solution (Notes.pdf, Sec. 5.1); adding the initial values of $\xi$ and of its derivative gives a Cauchy problem, whose unique solution is found by computing $D_1$ and $D_2$ from them ([Lecture 6, Slide 3]). The case of a double root is treated with critical damping, in Section 10.

General solution of the undamped oscillator Law: characteristic equation; direct substitution of two real trial functions; superposition Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.4; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.6; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.7; [Lecture 6, Slide 6]
$$\begin{aligned} m\ddot x + k\,x &= 0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 5.4)} \\ \ddot x + \omega_0^2\,x &= 0 \quad &\text{(divide by $m$, with $\omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m}$; Eq. 5.6)} \\ p^2 + \omega_0^2 &= 0 \quad &\text{(characteristic equation: $b_2 = 1$, $b_1 = 0$, $b_0 = \omega_0^2$)} \\ p &= \pm\,i\,\omega_0 \quad &\text{($p^2 = -\omega_0^2$ is negative: two imaginary roots)} \\ x &= D_1\exp(i\omega_0 t) + D_2\exp(-i\omega_0 t) \quad &\text{(general solution with two distinct roots; [Lecture 6, Slide 6])} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\cos(\omega_0 t) &= -\omega_0\sin(\omega_0 t) \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ \frac{d^2}{dt^2}\cos(\omega_0 t) &= -\omega_0^2\cos(\omega_0 t) \quad &\text{(chain rule again)} \\ \frac{d^2}{dt^2}\cos(\omega_0 t) + \omega_0^2\cos(\omega_0 t) &= 0 \quad &\text{(substitute in Eq. 5.6: the cosine is a solution)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\sin(\omega_0 t) &= \omega_0\cos(\omega_0 t) \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ \frac{d^2}{dt^2}\sin(\omega_0 t) &= -\omega_0^2\sin(\omega_0 t) \quad &\text{(chain rule again)} \\ \frac{d^2}{dt^2}\sin(\omega_0 t) + \omega_0^2\sin(\omega_0 t) &= 0 \quad &\text{(substitute: the sine is a solution)} \\ \frac{\sin(\omega_0 t)}{\cos(\omega_0 t)} &= \tan(\omega_0 t) \quad &\text{(not constant: the two solutions are independent)} \\ x &= C_1\cos(\omega_0 t) + C_2\sin(\omega_0 t) \quad &\text{(superposition, Eq. 5.5; Eq. 5.7)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\ddot x + \omega_0^2\,x = 0:\qquad p = \pm\,i\,\omega_0,\qquad x = C_1\cos(\omega_0 t) + C_2\sin(\omega_0 t)}$$

Units: $\omega_0$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, so $\omega_0 t$ is in radians; $C_1$, $C_2$ in $\mathrm m$

Meaning: the cosine and the sine of $\omega_0 t$ are two real, independent solutions, so their combination with two arbitrary constants is the general solution (Notes.pdf, Sec. 5.1). The complex form of the fifth row and this real form describe the same solutions; the passage from one to the other is Euler's relation, in Section 9.

Constants from the initial conditions Law: evaluation of the solution and of its first derivative at the initial instant Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.7; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.8; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.9; [Lecture 6, Slide 6]

At $t$ equal to zero the particle is at $x_0$ with velocity $\dot x_0$.

$$\begin{aligned} x(0) &= C_1\cos 0 + C_2\sin 0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 5.7 at $t = 0$)} \\ &= C_1 \quad &\text{($\cos 0 = 1$, $\sin 0 = 0$)} \\ C_1 &= x_0 \quad &\text{(first initial condition; Eq. 5.8)} \\ \dot x &= -C_1\,\omega_0\sin(\omega_0 t) + C_2\,\omega_0\cos(\omega_0 t) \quad &\text{(differentiate Eq. 5.7; chain rule on each term)} \\ \dot x(0) &= C_2\,\omega_0 \quad &\text{(at $t = 0$)} \\ C_2 &= \dot x_0/\omega_0 \quad &\text{(second initial condition, divided by $\omega_0$; Eq. 5.9)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{C_1 = x_0,\qquad C_2 = \frac{\dot x_0}{\omega_0},\qquad x = x_0\cos(\omega_0 t) + \frac{\dot x_0}{\omega_0}\sin(\omega_0 t)}$$

Units: $\mathrm m$ for $C_1$; $\mathrm{(m/s)/s^{-1}} = \mathrm m$ for $C_2$

Meaning: the cosine carries the initial displacement and the sine the initial velocity; a particle released from rest ($\dot x_0$ zero) oscillates as a pure cosine, and a particle kicked from the rest position ($x_0$ zero) as a pure sine.

Amplitude and initial phase Law: cosine of a sum; equal coefficients of independent functions; right triangle of the two constants Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.10; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.11; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.12; [Lecture 6, Slide 6]

The general solution is written as one cosine of amplitude $a$, not negative, and initial phase $\phi$. In the right triangle with hypotenuse $a$ and the angle $\phi$ at its vertex, the leg $C_1$ is adjacent to $\phi$ and the leg $-C_2$ is opposite to it.

$$\begin{aligned} a\cos(\omega_0 t + \phi) &= a\cos\phi\cos(\omega_0 t) - a\sin\phi\sin(\omega_0 t) \quad &\text{(cosine of a sum)} \\ C_1 &= a\cos\phi \quad &\text{(equal coefficients of $\cos(\omega_0 t)$ in Eq. 5.7 and Eq. 5.10; Eq. 5.11)} \\ C_2 &= -a\sin\phi \quad &\text{(equal coefficients of $\sin(\omega_0 t)$; Eq. 5.12)} \\ C_1^2 + C_2^2 &= a^2\cos^2\phi + a^2\sin^2\phi \quad &\text{(square both rows and add)} \\ &= a^2 \quad &\text{(Pythagoras)} \\ a &= \sqrt{C_1^2 + C_2^2} \quad &\text{(positive root)} \\ &= \sqrt{x_0^2 + \left(\dot x_0/\omega_0\right)^2} \quad &\text{(Eqs. 5.8 and 5.9)} \\ \tan\phi &= -\frac{C_2}{C_1} \quad &\text{(divide Eq. 5.12 by Eq. 5.11, sign changed)} \\ &= -\frac{\dot x_0}{\omega_0\,x_0} \quad &\text{(Eqs. 5.8 and 5.9)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{x = a\cos(\omega_0 t + \phi),\qquad C_1 = a\cos\phi,\ \ C_2 = -a\sin\phi,\qquad a = \sqrt{x_0^2 + \left(\dot x_0/\omega_0\right)^2},\ \ \tan\phi = -\frac{\dot x_0}{\omega_0\,x_0}}$$

Units: $a$ in $\mathrm m$; $\phi$ in radians; the tangent is a quotient of two lengths, dimensionless

Meaning: $a$ is the amplitude and $\phi$ the initial phase of the oscillator at $t$ equal to zero (Notes.pdf, Sec. 5.1); at that instant [Lecture 6, Slide 6] reads the same relations as $x_0$ equal to $a\cos\phi$ and $\dot x_0$ equal to $-a\,\omega_0\sin\phi$. The tangent alone leaves two possible angles; the right one is fixed by the signs of the legs: $\cos\phi$ has the sign of $x_0$ and $\sin\phi$ the sign of $-\dot x_0$.

Energy of the oscillation and the amplitude Law: conservation of mechanical energy evaluated on the solution Source: [Lecture 6, Slide 7]; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.10
$$\begin{aligned} E &= \tfrac12\,m\,\dot x^2 + \tfrac12\,k\,x^2 \quad &\text{(kinetic plus potential energy; [Lecture 6, Slide 7])} \\ \dot x &= -a\,\omega_0\sin(\omega_0 t + \phi) \quad &\text{(differentiate Eq. 5.10; chain rule)} \\ E &= \tfrac12\,m\,a^2\omega_0^2\sin^2(\omega_0 t + \phi) + \tfrac12\,k\,a^2\cos^2(\omega_0 t + \phi) \quad &\text{(substitute $x$ and $\dot x$)} \\ &= \tfrac12\,k\,a^2\sin^2(\omega_0 t + \phi) + \tfrac12\,k\,a^2\cos^2(\omega_0 t + \phi) \quad &\text{($m\,\omega_0^2 = k$)} \\ &= \tfrac12\,k\,a^2 \quad &\text{(Pythagoras)} \\ a &= \sqrt{2E/k} \quad &\text{(solve for $a$; the turning point of Eq. 5.3)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{E = \tfrac12\,k\,a^2,\qquad a = \sqrt{2E/k}}$$

Units: $\mathrm{(N/m)\,m^2} = \mathrm J$

Meaning: the energy is constant and splits between kinetic and potential energy as the squares of a sine and a cosine; the amplitude of Eq. 5.10 is the same constant $a$ introduced in Eq. 5.3, and the particle oscillates between $x$ equal to $-a$ and $a$ (Notes.pdf, Sec. 5.1).

Period and frequency Law: energy equation solved for the speed; change of the integration variable from time to position; trigonometric substitution; Barrow's rule Source: [Lecture 6, Slide 7]; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.27

In the half period in which the particle goes from $-a$ to $a$ its velocity is positive; the return takes the same time, because the speed depends only on $x$. $u$ is the substitution variable.

$$\begin{aligned} \tfrac12\,m\,\dot x^2 &= E - \tfrac12\,k\,x^2 \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.27 with the potential of the spring)} \\ \frac{dx}{dt} &= \sqrt{\frac{2E - k\,x^2}{m}} \quad &\text{(solve for the velocity, positive in this half)} \\ \frac{\tau}{2} &= \int_{-a}^{a}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{\left(2E - k\,x^2\right)/m}} \quad &\text{(change of variable $t \to x$: $dx = \dot x\,dt$; [Lecture 6, Slide 7])} \\ \sqrt{\frac{2E - k\,x^2}{m}} &= \sqrt{\frac{k\,a^2 - k\,x^2}{m}} \quad &\text{(the energy of Eq. 5.13: $2E = k\,a^2$)} \\ &= \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}\sqrt{a^2 - x^2} \quad &\text{(take out the common factor $k/m$)} \\ &= \omega_0\sqrt{a^2 - x^2} \quad &\text{(Eq. 5.23)} \\ \frac{\tau}{2} &= \frac{1}{\omega_0}\int_{-a}^{a}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}} \quad &\text{(substitute)} \\ x &= a\sin u,\qquad dx = a\cos u\,du \quad &\text{(substitution and its differential)} \\ \sqrt{a^2 - a^2\sin^2 u} &= a\cos u \quad &\text{(Pythagoras; $\cos u \geq 0$ for $u$ between $-\pi/2$ and $\pi/2$)} \\ \frac{\tau}{2} &= \frac{1}{\omega_0}\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\frac{a\cos u}{a\cos u}\,du \quad &\text{(limits: $x = -a$ gives $u = -\pi/2$, $x = a$ gives $u = \pi/2$)} \\ &= \frac{1}{\omega_0}\big[u\big]_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \quad &\text{(the integrand is one; antiderivative $u = \arcsin(x/a)$, as on the slide)} \\ &= \frac{1}{\omega_0}\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\right) \quad &\text{(Barrow)} \\ &= \frac{\pi}{\omega_0} \quad &\text{(arithmetic)} \\ \tau &= \frac{2\pi}{\omega_0} \quad &\text{(multiply by two)} \\ f &= \frac{1}{\tau} \quad &\text{(oscillations per unit time)} \\ &= \frac{\omega_0}{2\pi} \quad &\text{(Eq. 5.13)} \\ \cos\big(\omega_0(t + \tau) + \phi\big) &= \cos(\omega_0 t + \phi + 2\pi) \quad &\text{(check on Eq. 5.10: $\omega_0\tau = 2\pi$)} \\ &= \cos(\omega_0 t + \phi) \quad &\text{(the cosine has period $2\pi$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\tau = \frac{2\pi}{\omega_0},\qquad f = \frac{1}{\tau} = \frac{\omega_0}{2\pi}}$$

Units: $\tau$ in $\mathrm s$ ($\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s^{-1}}$); $f$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}} = \mathrm{Hz}$

Meaning: the motion is periodic, and its period does not depend on the amplitude $a$ (Notes.pdf, Sec. 5.1). The frequency $f$ counts oscillations per second and must not be confused with the angular frequency $\omega_0$, in radians per second. The linearised pendulum of Section 7 (Eq. 4.46) is an undamped harmonic oscillator with $\theta$ in place of $x$ and $g/\ell$ in place of the square of $\omega_0$, and the period of this box is then the one found there from its own integral.

Figure 18. Free undamped oscillation $x = a\cos(\omega_0 t + \phi)$: amplitude $a$, period $\tau = 2\pi/\omega_0$, and the constants $C_1 = a\cos\phi$, $C_2 = -a\sin\phi$ as the legs of a right triangle of hypotenuse $a$ (Notes.pdf Eqs. 5.10 to 5.12)..

9. Complex representation

It is often convenient to describe periodic phenomena with complex exponentials (Notes.pdf, Sec. 5.2; [Lecture 6, Slide 4]): a complex constant holds the two real constants of a solution, derivatives of exponentials are products, and the motion appears as the turning of an arrow in the complex plane. The imaginary unit is the italic $i$; the bold $\mathbf i$ remains the unit vector of $Ox$.

Euler's relation Law: derivative of a product; derivative of a complex exponential; a function with zero derivative is constant Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.16; [Lecture 6, Slide 4]

$\beta$ is a real variable (the notes call it $\theta$). The auxiliary function is the product of $\exp(-i\beta)$ and $\cos\beta + i\sin\beta$; for any complex constant $c$ the derivative of $\exp(c\,\beta)$ with respect to $\beta$ is $c\exp(c\,\beta)$.

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{d}{d\beta}\Big[\exp(-i\beta)\left(\cos\beta + i\sin\beta\right)\Big] &= -i\exp(-i\beta)\left(\cos\beta + i\sin\beta\right) + \exp(-i\beta)\left(-\sin\beta + i\cos\beta\right) \quad &\text{(product rule)} \\ &= \exp(-i\beta)\left(-i\cos\beta - i\cdot i\,\sin\beta - \sin\beta + i\cos\beta\right) \quad &\text{(expand: take out the common factor $\exp(-i\beta)$ and distribute $-i$)} \\ &= \exp(-i\beta)\left(-i\cos\beta + \sin\beta - \sin\beta + i\cos\beta\right) \quad &\text{($-i\cdot i = 1$)} \\ &= 0 \quad &\text{(the four terms cancel in pairs)} \\ \exp(-i\beta)\left(\cos\beta + i\sin\beta\right) &= \exp(0)\left(\cos 0 + i\sin 0\right) \quad &\text{(constant: equal to its value at $\beta = 0$)} \\ &= 1 \quad &\text{(arithmetic)} \\ \exp(i\beta) &= \cos\beta + i\sin\beta \quad &\text{(multiply by $\exp(i\beta)$; Eq. 5.16)} \\ \exp(-i\beta) &= \cos\beta - i\sin\beta \quad &\text{(replace $\beta$ by $-\beta$: the cosine is even, the sine odd)} \\ \cos\beta &= \frac{\exp(i\beta) + \exp(-i\beta)}{2} \quad &\text{(add the two rows and halve)} \\ \sin\beta &= \frac{\exp(i\beta) - \exp(-i\beta)}{2i} \quad &\text{(subtract them and divide by $2i$)} \\ \Re(z) &= \frac{z + z^*}{2},\qquad \Im(z) = \frac{z - z^*}{2i} \quad &\text{(the same steps for any complex $z$ and its conjugate)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\exp(i\beta) = \cos\beta + i\sin\beta,\qquad \cos\beta = \frac{\exp(i\beta) + \exp(-i\beta)}{2},\qquad \sin\beta = \frac{\exp(i\beta) - \exp(-i\beta)}{2i}}$$

Units: $\beta$ in radians; every term is dimensionless

Meaning: $\exp(i\beta)$ is the point of the unit circle at the angle $\beta$ from the real axis: its real part is the cosine and its imaginary part the sine. These are the useful relations of [Lecture 6, Slide 4].

Complex form of the free oscillation Law: a real solution equals its own conjugate; Euler's relation; polar form of a complex number Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.7; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.10; [Lecture 6, Slide 6]
$$\begin{aligned} x &= D_1\exp(i\omega_0 t) + D_2\exp(-i\omega_0 t) \quad &\text{(general solution, Section 8)} \\ x^* &= D_1^*\exp(-i\omega_0 t) + D_2^*\exp(i\omega_0 t) \quad &\text{(conjugate: the conjugate of $\exp(i\beta)$ is $\exp(-i\beta)$ for real $\beta$)} \\ D_2 &= D_1^* \quad &\text{($x$ real means $x^* = x$ at every $t$: equal coefficients of $\exp(-i\omega_0 t)$)} \\ x &= \tfrac12 A\exp(i\omega_0 t) + \tfrac12 A^*\exp(-i\omega_0 t) \quad &\text{(name $A$ twice $D_1$; Eq. 5.14)} \\ &= \tfrac12\left(z + z^*\right),\qquad z = A\exp(i\omega_0 t) \quad &\text{(the second term is the conjugate of the first)} \\ &= \Re(z) \quad &\text{(Euler box, last row)} \\ A &= C_1 - i\,C_2 \quad &\text{(Eq. 5.15)} \\ z &= \left(C_1 - i\,C_2\right)\left(\cos(\omega_0 t) + i\sin(\omega_0 t)\right) \quad &\text{(Euler's relation, Eq. 5.16)} \\ &= C_1\cos(\omega_0 t) + i\,C_1\sin(\omega_0 t) - i\,C_2\cos(\omega_0 t) - i\cdot i\,C_2\sin(\omega_0 t) \quad &\text{(expand the product)} \\ &= C_1\cos(\omega_0 t) + i\,C_1\sin(\omega_0 t) - i\,C_2\cos(\omega_0 t) + C_2\sin(\omega_0 t) \quad &\text{($-i\cdot i = 1$)} \\ &= C_1\cos(\omega_0 t) + C_2\sin(\omega_0 t) + i\left(C_1\sin(\omega_0 t) - C_2\cos(\omega_0 t)\right) \quad &\text{(group the real and the imaginary terms)} \\ \Re(z) &= C_1\cos(\omega_0 t) + C_2\sin(\omega_0 t) \quad &\text{(real part: Eq. 5.7 is recovered)} \\ A &= a\exp(i\phi) \quad &\text{(polar form, Eq. 5.17)} \\ z &= a\exp\big(i(\omega_0 t + \phi)\big) \quad &\text{(product of exponentials: the exponents add)} \\ \Re(z) &= a\cos(\omega_0 t + \phi) \quad &\text{(Euler's relation: Eq. 5.10 is recovered)} \\ a\cos\phi + i\,a\sin\phi &= C_1 - i\,C_2 \quad &\text{(Euler on Eq. 5.17, equal to Eq. 5.15)} \\ C_1 &= a\cos\phi,\qquad C_2 = -a\sin\phi \quad &\text{(equal real and imaginary parts: Eqs. 5.11 and 5.12)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{x = \tfrac12 A\exp(i\omega_0 t) + \tfrac12 A^*\exp(-i\omega_0 t) = \Re\big(A\exp(i\omega_0 t)\big),\qquad A = C_1 - i\,C_2 = a\exp(i\phi)}$$

Units: $A$, $z$, $C_1$, $C_2$ and $a$ in $\mathrm m$; exponents dimensionless

Meaning: the complex amplitude $A$ contains in itself the two independent constants of the solution, its modulus the amplitude and its argument the initial phase (Notes.pdf, Sec. 5.2). For a real solution the two coefficients of the exponentials are conjugate, half of $a\exp(i\phi)$ and half of $a\exp(-i\phi)$, as written on [Lecture 6, Slide 6].

Real and imaginary parts of a complex solution Law: linearity of the equation; the coefficients $m$ and $k$ are real Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.18
$$\begin{aligned} z &= \Re(z) + i\,\Im(z) \quad &\text{(any complex solution of Eq. 5.4)} \\ m\ddot z + k\,z &= m\,\frac{d^2\Re(z)}{dt^2} + k\,\Re(z) + i\left(m\,\frac{d^2\Im(z)}{dt^2} + k\,\Im(z)\right) \quad &\text{(differentiate term by term; group; $m$, $k$ real)} \\ 0 &= \left(m\,\frac{d^2\Re(z)}{dt^2} + k\,\Re(z)\right) + i\left(m\,\frac{d^2\Im(z)}{dt^2} + k\,\Im(z)\right) \quad &\text{($z$ is a solution; Eq. 5.18)} \\ m\,\frac{d^2\Re(z)}{dt^2} + k\,\Re(z) &= 0,\qquad m\,\frac{d^2\Im(z)}{dt^2} + k\,\Im(z) = 0 \quad &\text{(a complex number is zero when both its parts are, and both brackets are real)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{m\ddot z + k\,z = 0 \ \Longrightarrow\ \Re(z) \text{ and } \Im(z) \text{ each satisfy } m\ddot x + k\,x = 0}$$

Units: $\mathrm N$ in every bracket

Meaning: one may solve with complex exponentials, where every derivative is a multiplication, and take the real part at the end (Notes.pdf, Sec. 5.2). The argument works because the coefficients are real: it is also the reason why the forced oscillator of Section 11 can be solved with a complex force.

The phasor in the complex plane Law: polar form of the complex amplitude and of the exponent; modulus and argument of a product of exponentials Source: Notes.pdf Fig. 5.2; Notes.pdf, Sec. 5.2; [Lecture 6, Slide 4]

[Lecture 6, Slide 4] writes a general complex exponential with the complex amplitude $A$ and the eigenvalue $p$ split as $-\gamma + i\omega$: $\omega$ is the angular frequency and $\gamma$ the decay or damping rate. The free oscillation of this section is the case of $\gamma$ equal to zero and $\omega$ equal to $\omega_0$.

$$\begin{aligned} z &= A\exp(p\,t) \quad &\text{([Lecture 6, Slide 4])} \\ &= a\exp(i\phi)\exp\big((-\gamma + i\omega)\,t\big) \quad &\text{(polar form of $A$; $p = -\gamma + i\omega$)} \\ &= a\exp(-\gamma t)\exp\big(i(\omega t + \phi)\big) \quad &\text{(the exponents add; real and imaginary exponents grouped)} \\ \lvert z\rvert &= a\exp(-\gamma t) \quad &\text{($\lvert\exp(i\beta)\rvert = \sqrt{\cos^2\beta + \sin^2\beta} = 1$)} \\ \arg z &= \omega t + \phi \quad &\text{(argument of $\exp(i\beta)$ is $\beta$)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\arg z &= \omega \quad &\text{(rate at which the arrow turns)} \\ \Re(z) &= a\exp(-\gamma t)\cos(\omega t + \phi) \quad &\text{(Euler's relation: projection on the real axis)} \\ \lvert z\rvert &= a,\qquad \Re(z) = a\cos(\omega_0 t + \phi) \quad &\text{(free undamped oscillator: $\gamma = 0$, $\omega = \omega_0$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{z = a\exp(-\gamma t)\exp\big(i(\omega t + \phi)\big):\quad \lvert z\rvert = a\exp(-\gamma t),\quad \arg z = \omega t + \phi;\qquad \text{undamped: a circle of radius } a \text{ at the rate } \omega_0}$$

Units: $\lvert z\rvert$ in $\mathrm m$; $\omega$, $\gamma$ and the rate of the argument in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$

Meaning: the phasor, the arrow from $0$ to $z$, turns about the origin with angular velocity $\omega_0$ on a circle whose radius is the amplitude, starting at the initial phase; the solution is the projection of this circular motion on the real axis, which is why $\omega_0$ is called the angular frequency (Notes.pdf, Sec. 5.2). Exponentials with $\omega$ positive turn counterclockwise, and with $\gamma$ positive their modulus decays with time, so the arrow spirals in ([Lecture 6, Slide 4]): this is the damped oscillator of Section 10.

Figure 19. The complex solution as a phasor: it turns at the angular frequency on a circle of radius $a$ (left), or spirals in with modulus $a\exp(-\gamma t)$ when damped (right); the real part is the displacement (Notes.pdf Fig. 5.2; [Lecture 6, Slide 4])..

10. The damped harmonic oscillator

A viscous damper added to the spring-mass system exerts a force proportional and opposite to the velocity, with the proportionality constant $\lambda$ (Notes.pdf, Sec. 5.3); with $k$ and $\lambda$ positive and no applied force, the equation of motion is the free damped equation of the first box of Section 8 ([Lecture 6, Slide 5]). The damper is a non-conservative force, so the mechanical energy is no longer constant.

Energy dissipated by the damper Law: rate of change of the mechanical energy equals the power of the non-conservative forces (Section 5) Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.19; Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.5.1; [Lecture 2, Slide 19]

The spring force is conservative, with the potential of Section 8; the damper force is the non-conservative force.

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{dE}{dt} &= \mathbf F_\lambda\cdot\mathbf v_0^P \quad &\text{(Section 5: $dE_0/dt = \mathbf F_N\cdot\mathbf v_0^P$)} \\ &= \left(-\lambda\dot x\,\mathbf i\right)\cdot\left(\dot x\,\mathbf i\right) \quad &\text{(damper force, Eq. 5.19; velocity along $\mathbf i$)} \\ &= -\lambda\,\dot x^2 \quad &\text{($\mathbf i\cdot\mathbf i = 1$)} \\ E &= \tfrac12\,m\,\dot x^2 + \tfrac12\,k\,x^2 \quad &\text{(mechanical energy of the oscillator)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\frac{d}{dt}\left(\tfrac12\,m\,\dot x^2 + \tfrac12\,k\,x^2\right) = -\lambda\,\dot x^2 \leq 0}$$

Units: $\mathrm{(N\,s/m)(m/s)^2} = \mathrm{N\,m/s} = \mathrm W$

Meaning: the damper removes energy at every instant at which the particle moves, so the energy can only decrease, and its rate of change vanishes only at the instants of zero velocity. The oscillations must therefore die out, which the solutions below make precise.

Characteristic equation of the damped oscillator Law: trial exponential solution; quadratic formula; sign of the discriminant Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.20; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.21; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.22; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.23; [Lecture 6, Slide 5]
$$\begin{aligned} m\ddot x + \lambda\dot x + k\,x &= 0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 5.20: Section 8 with $F_x = 0$)} \\ x &= \exp(p\,t) \quad &\text{(trial solution, Section 8)} \\ \dot x &= p\exp(p\,t) \quad &\text{(chain rule: derivative of the exponential times the derivative $p$ of its exponent)} \\ \ddot x &= p^2\exp(p\,t) \quad &\text{(chain rule again)} \\ m\,p^2\exp(p\,t) + \lambda\,p\exp(p\,t) + k\exp(p\,t) &= 0 \quad &\text{(substitute the three rows in the first)} \\ \left(m\,p^2 + \lambda\,p + k\right)\exp(p\,t) &= 0 \quad &\text{(take out the common factor $\exp(p\,t)$)} \\ m\,p^2 + \lambda\,p + k &= 0 \quad &\text{(the exponential is never zero; Eq. 5.21)} \\ p^2 + 2\gamma\,p + \omega_0^2 &= 0 \quad &\text{(divide by $m$; Eq. 5.23; [Lecture 6, Slide 5])} \\ p &= \frac{-2\gamma \pm \sqrt{4\gamma^2 - 4\omega_0^2}}{2} \quad &\text{(quadratic formula)} \\ &= -\gamma \pm \sqrt{\gamma^2 - \omega_0^2} \quad &\text{(take the factor $4$ out of the root and divide by $2$; Eq. 5.22)} \\ \sqrt{\gamma^2 - \omega_0^2} &< \gamma \quad &\text{(when $\gamma > \omega_0$: the radicand is smaller than $\gamma^2$)} \\ -\gamma \pm \sqrt{\gamma^2 - \omega_0^2} &< 0 \quad &\text{(both real roots are then negative)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{p = -\gamma \pm \sqrt{\gamma^2 - \omega_0^2}:\quad \frac{\gamma}{\omega_0} < 1 \text{ complex conjugate},\quad \frac{\gamma}{\omega_0} = 1 \text{ double, } -\gamma,\quad \frac{\gamma}{\omega_0} > 1 \text{ real, both negative}}$$

Units: $p$, $\gamma$ and $\omega_0$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$; every term of the characteristic equation in $\mathrm{s^{-2}}$

Meaning: the roots are generally complex (Notes.pdf, Sec. 5.3), and the sign of the discriminant, that is, the damping ratio compared with one, separates three kinds of motion: small, critical and large damping. In every case their real part is negative, so every solution decays.

Small damping

Underdamped solution Law: complex conjugate roots; a real solution has conjugate coefficients; Euler's relation Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.24; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.25; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.26; [Lecture 6, Slide 8]
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{\gamma^2 - \omega_0^2} &= \sqrt{-\left(\omega_0^2 - \gamma^2\right)} \quad &\text{($\gamma < \omega_0$: the radicand is negative)} \\ &= i\,\omega,\qquad \omega = \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - \gamma^2} \quad &\text{($\sqrt{-1} = i$; Eq. 5.24)} \\ p_\pm &= -\gamma \pm i\,\omega \quad &\text{(the two roots; [Lecture 6, Slide 8])} \\ x &= D_1\exp\big((-\gamma + i\omega)\,t\big) + D_2\exp\big((-\gamma - i\omega)\,t\big) \quad &\text{(two distinct roots, Section 8)} \\ &= \tfrac12 A\exp(i\omega t - \gamma t) + \tfrac12 A^*\exp(-i\omega t - \gamma t) \quad &\text{($x$ real: $D_2 = D_1^*$, and $A$ is twice $D_1$, as in Section 9; Eq. 5.25)} \\ &= \Re\big[A\exp(i\omega t - \gamma t)\big] \quad &\text{(the second term is the conjugate of the first; Eq. 5.26)} \\ &= a\exp(-\gamma t)\,\Re\big[\exp(i\phi)\exp(i\omega t)\big] \quad &\text{($A = a\exp(i\phi)$; the real factor $a\exp(-\gamma t)$ comes out)} \\ &= a\exp(-\gamma t)\cos(\omega t + \phi) \quad &\text{(exponents add; Euler's relation)} \\ &= \exp(-\gamma t)\left[C_1\cos(\omega t) + C_2\sin(\omega t)\right] \quad &\text{(cosine of a sum, with $C_1 = a\cos\phi$, $C_2 = -a\sin\phi$)} \\ \omega^2 &= \omega_0^2 - \gamma^2 < \omega_0^2 \quad &\text{($\gamma$ is positive)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{x = a\exp(-\gamma t)\cos(\omega t + \phi) = \exp(-\gamma t)\left[C_1\cos(\omega t) + C_2\sin(\omega t)\right],\qquad \omega = \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - \gamma^2} < \omega_0}$$

Units: $a$, $C_1$, $C_2$ in $\mathrm m$; $\gamma t$ and $\omega t$ dimensionless

Meaning: the solution is an oscillation with the exponentially decreasing amplitude $a\exp(-\gamma t)$ and the angular frequency $\omega$ of the damped oscillator, always smaller than the frequency $\omega_0$ of the undamped one (Notes.pdf, Sec. 5.3.1; Notes.pdf Fig. 5.3): the oscillatory behaviour of the ideal case, with a slightly different frequency, damped with the decay rate $\gamma$ ([Lecture 6, Slide 8]).

Erratum to Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.26: position of a bracket

The last form of Eq. 5.26 is printed with the real part closed before the factor $\exp(i\omega t)$, so that this factor multiplies a real number from outside the real part and the printed expression is complex, not a displacement. The real part must enclose both exponentials of unit modulus, as in the box above and on [Lecture 6, Slide 8], where the factor $a\exp(-\gamma t)$ is outside and $\exp(i\phi)\exp(i\omega t)$ inside. Check: with the printed bracket, for $\gamma$ equal to zero, $\phi$ equal to zero and $\omega t$ equal to $\pi/2$ the expression is $a$ times $i$, a purely imaginary number, while the corrected one gives $a\cos(\pi/2)$, zero.

Constants of the underdamped solution from the initial conditions Law: evaluation of the solution and of its first derivative at the initial instant Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.26; [Lecture 6, Slide 8]; [Lecture 6, Slide 3]
$$\begin{aligned} x(0) &= \exp(0)\left[C_1\cos 0 + C_2\sin 0\right] \quad &\text{(last form of the box above at $t = 0$)} \\ &= C_1 \quad &\text{(arithmetic)} \\ C_1 &= x_0 \quad &\text{(first initial condition)} \\ \dot x &= -\gamma\exp(-\gamma t)\left[C_1\cos(\omega t) + C_2\sin(\omega t)\right] + \exp(-\gamma t)\left[-C_1\,\omega\sin(\omega t) + C_2\,\omega\cos(\omega t)\right] \quad &\text{(product rule; chain rule on each factor)} \\ \dot x(0) &= -\gamma\,C_1 + \omega\,C_2 \quad &\text{(at $t = 0$)} \\ C_2 &= \frac{\dot x_0 + \gamma\,x_0}{\omega} \quad &\text{(second initial condition with $C_1 = x_0$; divide by $\omega$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{C_1 = x_0,\qquad C_2 = \frac{\dot x_0 + \gamma\,x_0}{\omega}}$$

Units: $\mathrm m$ for both: $\mathrm{(m/s + s^{-1}\,m)/s^{-1}}$

Meaning: without damping ($\gamma$ zero, $\omega$ equal to $\omega_0$) these are Eqs. 5.8 and 5.9. A particle released from rest still needs a small sine term, because the damper slows it from the start.

Relaxation time and quality factor Law: decay of the amplitude $a\exp(-\gamma t)$; definitions of the notes; first-order expansion for small damping Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.27; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.28; Notes.pdf, Sec. 5.3.1; [Lecture 6, Slide 8]
$$\begin{aligned} a\exp(-\gamma\,t_r) &= a\,e^{-1} \quad &\text{(the amplitude falls by the factor $1/e$ in the time $t_r$)} \\ t_r &= \frac{1}{\gamma} \quad &\text{(equal exponents)} \\ &= \frac{2m}{\lambda} \quad &\text{($\gamma = \lambda/(2m)$; Eq. 5.27)} \\ Q &= \frac{\omega_0}{2\gamma} \quad &\text{(definition of the quality factor; Eq. 5.28; [Lecture 6, Slide 8])} \\ &= \frac{m\,\omega_0}{\lambda} \quad &\text{(the same substitution; Eq. 5.28)} \\ \frac{a\exp\big(-\gamma\,(t + 2\pi/\omega)\big)}{a\exp(-\gamma t)} &= \exp\left(-\frac{2\pi\gamma}{\omega}\right) \quad &\text{(amplitude after one period $2\pi/\omega$, over the amplitude before it)} \\ \omega &= \omega_0\left(1 - \frac{\gamma^2}{\omega_0^2}\right)^{1/2} \quad &\text{(take $\omega_0^2$ out of the root)} \\ &= \omega_0\left(1 - \frac{\gamma^2}{2\,\omega_0^2} + \dots\right) \quad &\text{(binomial expansion; the correction is of second order in $\gamma/\omega_0$)} \\ \exp\left(-\frac{2\pi\gamma}{\omega}\right) &\simeq \exp\left(-\frac{2\pi\gamma}{\omega_0}\right) \quad &\text{(small damping: keep $\omega \simeq \omega_0$)} \\ &= \exp\left(-\frac{\pi}{Q}\right) \quad &\text{($2\gamma/\omega_0 = 1/Q$)} \\ \frac{t_r}{2\pi/\omega} &= \frac{\omega}{2\pi\gamma} \quad &\text{(number of periods in a relaxation time)} \\ &\simeq \frac{\omega_0}{2\pi\gamma} \quad &\text{($\omega \simeq \omega_0$)} \\ &= \frac{Q}{\pi} \quad &\text{(definition of $Q$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{t_r = \frac{1}{\gamma} = \frac{2m}{\lambda},\qquad Q = \frac{m\,\omega_0}{\lambda} = \frac{\omega_0}{2\gamma};\qquad \text{per period: } \exp\left(-\frac{2\pi\gamma}{\omega}\right) \simeq \exp\left(-\frac{\pi}{Q}\right),\quad \frac{t_r}{2\pi/\omega} \simeq \frac{Q}{\pi}}$$

Units: $t_r$ in $\mathrm s$ ($1/\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{kg/(N\,s/m)} = \mathrm s$); $Q$ dimensionless ($\mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}/(N\,s/m)} = 1$)

Meaning: small damping means a large quality factor (Notes.pdf, Sec. 5.3.1). For $Q$ equal to $10$ ($\gamma/\omega_0$ equal to $0.05$) one period multiplies the amplitude by $0.730$ (the approximation $\exp(-\pi/Q)$ gives $0.730$ as well), and a relaxation time holds about $3.2$ periods.

Large damping
